reply: Guided tour of Barnard's Star: 7 steps. Touch any control to take over.

steps.say: This is Barnard's Star: Red dwarf about 1.8 pc away with the largest known proper motion. SPHEREx imaged it on 3 dates in D2, from 2025-08-29 to 2026-08-22 (358 days). The view starts on D2 (1.1–1.62 µm).

Play the dates in order. At 10.4″/yr it should move about 1.6 px (pixels are 6.2″) between the first and last date; the crosshair marks where the catalog motion puts it on each date. Measured between 2025-08-29 and 2026-08-22, the dates where it is bright enough to fit: 1.72 px, against 1.6 px expected for that interval.
Blink compares two dates directly: 2025-08-29 against 2026-08-22. A moving source jumps; a still one only changes brightness, if at all.

The six detectors cover 0.75–5.0 µm, from left to right. In the measurements it is detected in D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, D6. Its D5/D4 flux ratio (methane index) is 1.0; ordinary stars sit near 0.5–1.5 and methane-rich cold dwarfs far above.
Its core is saturated in some detectors: those pixels have no data and are shown in purple. The flags layer marks the pixels the SPHEREx pipeline flagged.
The rule-based engine labels it a star; that agrees with the catalog type (star, SIMBAD).
2 of 14 sources in this field need a human look. The first one, Gaia DR3 4472835983521060096, is flagged for: Only in one date. Is it real or an artefact?
